newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African MP complains at EU ostrich ban.
newsitem.headline: S.African MP complains at EU ostrich ban.

text.p: A South African parliamentarian on Friday called the European Union ban on South African ostrich meat over health fears irresponsible and inappropriate.

"It is obvious that the action of the EU was based on their trying to equate this outbreak with the English Mad Cow disease," said Reggie Oliphant, who represents the capital of South Africa's ostrich industry in the town of Oudtshoorn.
"Such an equation is quite obviously completely erroneous," Oliphant, from the ruling African National Congress, said in a statement.
"I appeal to all concerned in the ostrich industry to assist me and the government to ensure that this ban is not put into effect...it is both inappropriate and irresponsible."

The EU on Thursday banned imports of ostrich meat or live ostriches from South Africa because of an outbreak of Congo fever among ostrich abattoir workers in Oudtshoorn last month. One worker died and 16 others were treated in hospital.
Ostrich meat gained popularity in Europe after scientists said Mad Cow disease might be passed on to humans who ate beef from infected animals.
The EU ostrich ban is to be reviewed in February, or sooner if new evidence emerges about the effect of eating ostriches that have been bitten by the ticks that carry Congo fever.

A spokesman for the Little Karoo Cooperative in Oudtshoorn, which produces about 80 percent of world ostrich products, said the cooperative had decided to make funds available so research into health implications of eating ostrich meat could begin immediately.

He said the abattoir, closed last month when the disease broke out, would reopen on November 27. Hides and feathers, 80 percent of the value of an ostrich, are not affected by the ban. Meat from slaughtered ostriches would be frozen for possible future consumption, the spokesman said.
